findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is. After this sentence, however, the page says almost nothing more about Athena itself.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page does say why the study exists. But the study only shows Athena reading and explaining another project. It does not show what the lede sells: turning a request into a change, having a second model check the work, and recording costs. A newcomer sees no example of Athena's main job.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of firstmate, a different tool. It uses terms like exit 75, places-held, and close-pending. This suits someone studying firstmate. A newcomer who arrived at Athena's site will likely have to skim past it to find out what Athena is for.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (cards t1–t11)

findings.text: A next step is offered at the top and linked to its section, so the reader is not left without a way forward.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" linking to #next-steps

findings.text: The install steps are too short to follow on their own. There is no clone command, no list of prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or AI model credentials), and no description of what `athena ask` produces or where. The reader has to go to the GitHub repository to get started.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Jargon is defined before it is used and again in the glossary. Where the source is silent, the page says so instead of guessing (for example "in scope"). This keeps the dense content readable.
These limits are stated honestly. But a newcomer judging Athena may read "a first reading ... missed these paths" and "none was run" as weak evidence of the capability the page is meant to show.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths ... none was run, so no run confirmed that a script behaves as its header says."

findings.text: Each statement links to exact file lines at a pinned commit, so a reader can check the page's claims. This shows Athena's traceability concretely, even if the subject matter is not what a newcomer came for.
findings.source: Claims and sources: links such as "bin/fm-spawn.sh:194-197" at the pinned commit
